payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
In 1981, Dave Smith and Chet Wood of Sequential Circuits presented a paper at the Audio Engineering Society's 70th convention in New York. Its title was "The 'USI', or Universal Synthesizer Interface," and its abstract is modest for a document that changed how records get made. It calls the specification preliminary and says the interface has not been tested. The authors asked for criticism and for competing proposals.

In early 1982, at the NAMM show, the instrument trade's annual fair, Smith called a meeting of the other makers. By his own later account he told them that everyone needed to design something together and that it did not have to be his version. Few stayed with it: four Japanese companies and Sequential.

The standard that shipped was not the one proposed

At the time each maker linked its own machines its own way. Oberheim had a fast connection of its own between its instruments, and its founder worried that the new proposal would be too slow. Before the proposal shipped, the Japanese companies changed it substantially. The original had used ordinary quarter-inch jacks, and the five-pin connector was their suggestion. Smith said afterward that many of the changes came from them. The name went too. What came out was MIDI, the Musical Instrument Digital Interface: a five-pin cable and a short list of messages, such as which key was pressed and how hard.

A · Proposed, 1981

One company's draft

Written at Sequential. Quarter-inch jacks, and untested by its own description.

B · Shipped, 1983

Five companies' revision

Reworked with four Japanese makers. Five-pin connector, shown working between two rivals' instruments.

In January 1983, back at NAMM, a Sequential Prophet-600 was cabled to a Roland Jupiter-6, and the two worked together. Sequential had tested its synthesizer only against a second Prophet. By the account of the company's own sound designer, nobody there knew whether it would work with the Roland until it did. Two companies that fought for the same customers put their instruments on one cable in public, running a design neither could call its own.

Nobody was charged, on purpose

No license fee was attached. Smith gave the reason in a 2013 interview: the goal was complete participation, so the companies decided not to charge anyone who wanted to use it. The president of the manufacturers' association gave the logic in the same article. The interface earned no revenue itself, but it made the products that carried it more valuable, and every company at that table sold instruments. The cable was never the product.

It did not protect them. By its own account Sequential ceased operations in 1987, and its name and assets went to Yamaha. The standard never stopped shipping.

Fortune dated the sale to Yamaha to 1988 in its 2013 profile. The company site says operations ceased in 1987.

An open format costs its author the final say

I have argued that the signing method has to be open while products built on it stay closed. That argument concerns the format. The 1981 abstract concerns the person holding the first draft, and it describes a cost my argument never mentioned.

Publishing a record format for proof of origin under an open license is the easy half. The license does that work in a line: anyone may take it. The harder half is what the 1981 abstract conceded before anyone had agreed to anything, which is that the version adopted might be someone else's. In the event it was revised by competitors and renamed, and that outcome counted as the proposal succeeding. A format that has to stay the way its author wrote it tends to stay with its author.

The parties usually nominated to adopt a provenance record have reasons to wait. Streaming platforms grew by treating every upload alike, and the makers of recording software fear owning every false claim their tool appears to vouch for. Whoever does go first will want changes. I do not know yet which of my own choices I would defend and which I would trade for a second name on the specification, and 1981 suggests that question gets asked before the format is finished.

References

Wagner, K. "One of tech's most successful inventors never made a cent." Fortune, April 11, 2013. fortune.com

payload.title: The proposal that became MIDI asked to be replaced
